newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Blast reminds recovering Yeltsin of social ills.
newsitem.headline: Blast reminds recovering Yeltsin of social ills.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, recovering rapidly from his heart operation, got a grim reminder from a deadly explosion on Sunday of problems awaiting his return to work.
At least 11 people died when a blast ripped through a crowd attending a cemetery commemorative service in what police said seemed to be a settling of mafia scores.

Crime has risen sharply in post-Soviet Russia and Yeltsin's government has been blamed for allowing things to get out of hand. It will be one of the issues on the agenda when the president, out of the Kremlin over four months, gets back to his desk.

Doctors said on Sunday Yeltsin was in a "satisfactory condition" after Tuesday's seven-hour operation and was being allowed to move around more in his suite of rooms in the elite Central Clinical Hospital.

Chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov told Itar-Tass news agency that Yeltsin could leave hospital after November 20 for the exclusive Barvikha sanatorium, a complex of government rest homes outside the Russian capital.
Yeltsin, re-elected on July 3 for a second term, has spent only a few days in the Kremlin since the poll and waited for weeks for the bypass operation.
Top surgeon Renat Akchurin told Russian television on Saturday that doctors would remove the sutures in the next 10 or 12 days.
"He should not run, jump or play tennis, but he will be capable of talking with people, issuing orders," Akchurin said. "I have not seen a sharper mind."
Russia's social and economic situation has deteriorated sharply while the president has been away and Kremlin power struggles worsened while he waited for doctors to set a date for the operation.
The International Monetary Fund twice delayed handing over tranches of a $10 billion loan, most recently because of concerns about tax evasion and tax arrears.

Officials say the tax arrears mean the government is unable to pay its bills, which in turn means workers are not paid. Tens of thousands of them demonstrated across Russia last week, demanding that arrears are paid.

The economic hardships have taken their toll on Yeltsin's supporters in regional elections being held across Russia. Yeltsin appointee Oleg Savchenko crashed to defeat in the central Russian region of Kaluga at the weekend.
He was defeated by Valery Sudarenkov, centrist who was backed by local communists.
"The main reason for Savchenko's defeat is a difficult social and economic situation in the region, delays in payment of pensions and wages and rising crime," Itar-Tass news agency said.
Communist parliamentarian Viktor Zorkaltsev told a news conference on Sunday that the results of the election reflected is "popular reaction to the deceipt of July 3."
He said nine of the 19 regional elections held so far this year had been won by communist-backed candidates, seven had been won by government-backed candidates and two polls were invalid.
The final election was won by a member of extreme nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky's Liberal Democratic Party.
The local elections, being held in most of Russia's 89 regions over a six-month period ending next February, allow voters to select a new regional governor.
But the polls are important on a national level as well because the regional governors become members of the Federation Council upper house of parliament.

The State Duma lower house is already dominated by communists and their allies, who have stalled Russia's 1997 budget plans, demanding that the government rethink its revenue forecasts. The Duma is likely to discuss the budget on Friday.
